steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on cold-start bundle recommendation, presenting our method CoHeat (popularity-based coalescence and curriculum heating) and its contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: recommender systems, bundle recommendation, cold-start bundles
- Existing bundle recommendation methods are built for warm-start
- Cold-start item recommendation methods and why they fall short for bundles
- Our method: CoHeat
- Contributions (problem, method, experiments) and code

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - recommender systems: personalized list of relevant items on online platforms
  - bundle recommendation: attention from academia and industry; one-stop convenience for users
  - new bundles constantly created on the Web for marketing purposes -> cold-start bundle recommendation crucial
  - opening question: how to recommend cold-start bundles to users?
- Existing bundle recommendation = warm-start
  - matrix factorization-based approaches; graph learning-based approaches
  - assume all bundles have historical interactions with users
  - efficacy drops in cold-start (bundles without interactions)
  - reason: rely on user-bundle interaction history to find collaborative signals
- Cold-start item recommendation
  - cold-start problem studied extensively; align behavior representations with content representations
  - generative methods: model generation of item behavior representations via mean squared error, metric learning, or adversarial loss
  - dropout-based: randomly drop behavior embedding during training -> robustness
  - contrastive learning-based (recent): reduce discrepancy between behavior and content distributions; superior performance
  - fail for bundles: cannot leverage user-item interactions to represent bundles
  - nobody explicitly considers skewed user-bundle interaction distribution (Figure 1(a))
  - unpopular bundles: aligning weak behavior reps with content reps amplifies biases, hard to learn; trade warm-start performance for cold-start (Figure 2)
- CoHeat (Popularity-based Coalescence and Curriculum Heating)
  - two graph-based views: user-bundle view (user-bundle interactions), user-item view (bundle affiliations + user-item interactions)
  - popularity-based coalescence: uses both views; emphasizes user-item view for less popular bundles (Figures 1(b), 1(c))
  - curriculum learning: training focus moves gradually from user-bundle view to user-item view
  - contrastive learning to align the two views
- Contributions
  - Problem: first work on cold-start bundle recommendation; significant real-world impact
  - Method: CoHeat, accurate; handles highly skewed interactions; recommends cold bundles via affiliations
  - Experiments: state of the art, up to 193% higher nDCG@20 than best competitor in cold-start; competitive in warm-start (Figure 2, Table 2)
  - code: https://github.com/snudatalab/CoHeat

steps.text:
How can we recommend cold-start bundles to users? Recommender systems are important in online platforms because they give users a personalized list of relevant items. Lately bundle recommendation got a lot of attention in both academia and industry, since it lets providers offer items to users with one-stop convenience. Especially, recommending new bundles to users (i.e. cold-start bundle recommendation) has become crucial as the Web evolves, because new bundles are constantly created on the Web for various marketing purposes.

Bundle recommendation has advanced mostly through matrix factorization-based approaches and graph learning-based approaches. But these were developed for a warm-start setting, where all bundles already have historical interactions with users. So they work less well in cold-start scenarios, where some bundles have no historical interactions at all. The reason is that warm-start methods depend a lot on the historical user-bundle interactions to find collaborative signals between users and bundles.

- cold-start problem in item recommendation studied a lot; align behavior and content representations
- generative methods (mean squared error, metric learning, adversarial loss); dropout-based methods; contrastive learning-based methods (recent, best)
- fail for bundles: can't use user-item interactions to represent bundles
- nobody considers skewed user-bundle distribution (Figure 1(a)); unpopular bundles -> biases amplified, warm-start performance sacrificed (Figure 2)
- CoHeat: two graph views (user-bundle, user-item); popularity-based coalescence (Figures 1(b), 1(c)); curriculum learning from user-bundle to user-item view; contrastive learning to align views

- code: https://github.com/snudatalab/CoHeat

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
How can we recommend cold-start bundles to users? Recommender systems are important in online platforms because they give users a personalized list of relevant items. Lately bundle recommendation got a lot of attention in both academia and industry, since it lets providers offer items to users with one-stop convenience. Especially, recommending new bundles to users (i.e. cold-start bundle recommendation) has become crucial as the Web evolves, because new bundles are constantly created on the Web for various marketing purposes.

Bundle recommendation has advanced mostly through matrix factorization-based approaches and graph learning-based approaches. But these were developed for a warm-start setting, where all bundles already have historical interactions with users. So they work less well in cold-start scenarios, where some bundles have no historical interactions at all. The reason is that warm-start methods depend a lot on the historical user-bundle interactions to find collaborative signals between users and bundles.

On the other hand, the cold-start problem in item recommendation has been studied a lot, and the focus is on aligning behavior representations with content representations. For example, generative methods tried to model how item behavior representations are generated, using mean squared error, metric learning, or adversarial loss. Dropout-based methods tried to make the model robust to behavior information by randomly dropping the behavior embedding during training. More recently, contrastive learning-based methods showed superior performance by reducing the discrepancy between the distributions of behavior and content information of items. However, these existing cold-start item recommendation methods do not get high performance in bundle recommendation, because they are not able to effectively use the user-item historical interactions when they represent bundles. Also, none of the existing works explicitly considered that user-bundle interactions have a skewed distribution, which is a pivotal aspect in bundle recommendation as shown in Figure 1(a). For unpopular bundles, aligning behavior representations that come from insufficient historical information with content representations amplifies the inherent biases and makes it hard to learn meaningful representations. This ends up sacrificing the performance on a warm-start setting to get better performance on a cold-start setting (see Figure 2).

In this paper we propose CoHeat (Popularity-based Co alescence and Curriculum Heat ing) for cold-start bundle recommendation. CoHeat builds representations of users and bundles with two different graph-based views, a user-bundle view and a user-item view. The user-bundle view is based on historical interactions between users and bundles, and the user-item view is based on bundle affiliations and historical interactions between users and items. To deal with the extremely skewed distribution shown in Figure 1(a), CoHeat uses both views in its predictions through our popularity-based coalescence. This puts more emphasis on the user-item view for less popular bundles, since they give richer information than the sparse user-bundle view, as shown in Figures 1(b) and 1(c). Also, to learn the user-item view representations well, which are fully used for cold-start bundles, CoHeat uses a curriculum learning approach that gradually moves the training focus from the user-bundle view to the user-item view. CoHeat also uses a contrastive learning approach to align the representations of the two views.

Our contributions are as follows:

- • Problem. As far as we know, this is the first work that deals with the cold-start problem in bundle recommendation, which is a challenging problem with significant impact in real-world scenarios.

- • Method. We propose CoHeat, an accurate method for cold-start bundle recommendation. CoHeat learns user and bundle representations while handling highly skewed interactions, so it can recommend cold bundles through their affiliations.

- • Experiments. We show in experiments that CoHeat gives the state-of-the-art performance, with up to 193% higher nDCG @20 than the best competitor in cold-start scenarios, while keeping competitive performance in warm-start scenarios (see Figure 2 and Table 2).

The code is available at https://github.com/snudatalab/CoHeat.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
How can we recommend cold-start bundles to users? Recommender systems have been significant in online platforms, providing users with a personalized list of relevant items [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]. In recent years, bundle recommendation has received significant attention in both academia and industry since it enables providers to offer items to users with one-stop convenience [8]. In particular, recommending new bundles to users (i.e. cold-start bundle recommendation) has become crucial with the Web’s evolution, as new bundles are constantly created on the Web for various marketing purposes [9].

In recent years, bundle recommendation has advanced mainly through matrix factorization-based approaches [10,11,9,12,13] and graph learning-based approaches [14,15,16,8,17,18,19,20,21]. However, they have been developed for a warm-start setting, where all bundles already have historical interactions with users. Consequently, their efficacy decreases in cold-start scenarios, where certain bundles have no historical interactions. This is because warm-start methods rely heavily on historical information of user-bundle interactions to discern collaborative signals between users and bundles [22].

On the other hand, the cold-start problem [23] in item recommendation has been extensively studied, with a focus on aligning behavior representations with content representations. For instance, generative methods have aimed to model the generation of item behavior representations using mean squared error [24,25], metric learning [26], or adversarial loss [27]. Dropout-based methods [28,29] have aimed to improve robustness to behavior information by randomly dropping the behavior embedding in the training phase. More recently, contrastive learning-based methods [30,31] have shown superior performance by reducing the discrepancy between the distributions of behavior and content information of items. However, the existing methods for cold-start item recommendation fail to achieve high performance in bundle recommendation because they cannot effectively leverage the user-item historical interactions when representing bundles. Furthermore, none of the existing works have explicitly considered the skewed distribution of user-bundle interactions, which is a pivotal aspect in bundle recommendation as shown in Figure 1(a). For unpopular bundles, aligning behavior representations from insufficient historical information with content representations amplifies inherent biases and makes it difficult to learn meaningful representations; this results in sacrificing the performance on a warm-start setting to improve the performance on a cold-start setting (see Figure 2).

In this paper, we propose CoHeat (Popularity-based Co alescence and Curriculum Heat ing) to address cold-start bundle recommendation. CoHeat constructs representations of users and bundles using two distinct graph-based views: a user-bundle view and a user-item view. The user-bundle view is based on historical interactions between users and bundles, whereas the user-item view is based on bundle affiliations and historical interactions between users and items. To handle the extremely skewed distribution shown in Figure 1(a), CoHeat strategically leverages both views in its predictions through our proposed popularity-based coalescence; this emphasizes the user-item view for less popular bundles since they provide richer information than the sparse user-bundle view, as shown in Figures 1(b) and 1(c). In addition, to effectively learn the user-item view representations which are fully used for cold-start bundles, CoHeat exploits a curriculum learning approach that gradually shifts the training focus from the user-bundle view to the user-item view. CoHeat further exploits a contrastive learning approach to align the representations of the two views.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- • Problem. To our knowledge, this is the first work that tackles the cold-start problem in bundle recommendation, a challenging problem with significant impact in real-world scenarios.

- • Method. We propose CoHeat, an accurate cold-start bundle recommendation method. CoHeat learns user and bundle representations by addressing highly skewed interactions, which enables it to recommend cold bundles through their affiliations.

- • Experiments. We experimentally show that CoHeat provides state-of-the-art performance, achieving up to 193% higher nDCG @20 than the best competitor in cold-start scenarios while maintaining competitive performance in warm-start scenarios (see Figure 2 and Table 2).

The code is available at https://github.com/snudatalab/CoHeat.
